"You look at problems through one lens. Many computations are a loop: the next state is computed from the current one,
so step 1,000 cannot start until step 999 ends, and when the state is small most of a GPU sits idle. Such a loop can
sometimes be computed all at once: guess every state, check every step in parallel against the one before, correct
all the errors together, and repeat until nothing changes. The result is exactly what the loop would give. It pays only
when the system forgets its past, so that early errors fade: damped, dissipative or mixing dynamics, or a long sampling
chain. It fails when small errors grow, as in chaotic systems. Before spending, measure forgetfulness: start two runs a
hair apart and see whether they converge or drift apart. A good candidate has a step-by-step loop, a small state (a
handful to a few hundred numbers), a long run (thousands of steps or more), forgetful dynamics, and few runs needed; if
thousands of runs are needed, run them side by side instead. The method does more total arithmetic and wins only on how
long one answer takes. Before proposing anything, check whether a strong GPU method for this already exists; rebuilding
it wins nothing. Write down your predictions and how you could be wrong before any test, and compare against a tuned
sequential baseline and against many independent copies run side by side.

Here is a research problem as it was first written down, with the question it belongs to.
Root question: generative pipeline for discovery of single phase immersion coolants
Problem:
**IC-V1 · Force-field error floor for coolant MD: an enlarged C10–C50 benchmark scored against measurement.** seed pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: not the lever · PASS

**Question.** Will graphics-card molecular simulations using Green–Kubo on C10–C50 hydrocarbons and esters rank immersion coolants' viscosity and thermal conductivity the same way measurements do?

**What is known.** Ogbomo and colleagues, in 2026, used Green–Kubo molecular dynamics to compute viscosity and thermal conductivity for eight C10–C50 molecules at 40 °C and compared with measurements [s_ogbomo_md]. Whether the error is a correctable bias or a random floor that caps ranking, and how rank agreement holds over hundreds of molecules [s_ogbomo_db].

**Hypothesis.** Green–Kubo MD with one fixed force field has a chemistry-dependent error floor near 25 percent that more molecules cannot remove [s_ogbomo_res].

**If compute is the lever.** At 120 molecules, held-out viscosity error after bias correction falls below 15 percent and rank correlation with measurement exceeds 0.9 [s_ogbomo_res].

**If not.** Held-out viscosity error stays above 25 percent and rank correlation below 0.7 at every set size, capping candidate ranking [s_ogbomo_res].

**Test.** One LAMMPS LOPLS-AA Green–Kubo protocol at 40 °C, six five-nanosecond replicas per molecule, run on 8, 24, 48 then 120 molecules from the public 835-molecule reference set, scored only against measured viscosity and thermal conductivity [s_ogbomo_db].

*Compute axis.* Benchmark molecules scored against measured viscosity and thermal conductivity: 8–120 molecules, 4 levels. Closest prior: 8 [s_ogbomo_md], beyond it.

*Restructuring.* none.

**Check first.** Repeat the published eight-molecule Green–Kubo run first: density within 4% for seven molecules and thermal conductivity over-predicted for all eight [s_ogbomo_res]. Tolerance: same bias signs for viscosity and thermal conductivity; density error within 4 percentage points of the published error; per-molecule viscosity within 20% of the reference value.

**Would not show.** Shows transport-property error only at 40 °C for pure liquids between 1 and 50 mPa·s, not blends or sold coolants. Cannot show ranking behaviour beyond 120 molecules.

*Cost.* Plans $940.98 of the $1,000 budget over 59 machine-hours, leaving $59.02. Main guess: assumed MD throughput per GPU [p], measured after $36.20 of spend; the budget is reached if it is 1.1× lower. 3 cost flags in the block.

Find where this problem stops more compute from helping, or where more compute only buys more of the same. Then look for reframings: changes to what is measured, the unit of work, the objective or the order of steps that would let more compute change the answer. Give up to three. End each with one question someone could investigate: specific, answerable by a measurement, and naming what is measured. For each, give the cheapest measurement that would answer it or show it is not worth pursuing, with a rough cost. Decide from the text above and what you know; do not use tools.

Return only one JSON value, with no other text, that matches this JSON Schema:

Let me understand the task. The system prompt is about parallel-in-time / ParaReal-style methods: many computations are sequential loops; sometimes you can compute all at once by guessing states, checking in parallel, correcting (parareal). It pays when dynamics are forgetful (damped, dissipative, mixing, or long sampling chains); fails for chaotic. Measure forgetfulness: two runs a hair apart. Good candidate: step-by-step loop, small state, long run, forgetful dynamics, few runs. Method does more total arithmetic, wins on wall-clock latency. Check strong GPU methods exist first. Compare against tuned sequential baseline and many independent replicas side-by-side.

Then the research problem: IC-V1 force-field error floor for coolant MD: Green–Kubo MD on C10–C50 hydrocarbons and esters to compute viscosity and thermal conductivity at 40 °C, rank against measurement. Six 5-ns replicas per molecule, LAMMPS LOPLS-AA, 8–120 molecules, ~$941 of $1000 budget, 59 machine-hours.

Task: Find where this problem stops more compute from helping, or where more compute only buys more of the same. Then find reframings: changes to what is measured, the unit of work, the objective, or the order of steps that would let more compute change the answer. Up to three. Each ends with one specific, measurable question. For each, give the cheapest measurement that would answer it or show it's not worth pursuing, with rough cost. No tools. Return only JSON matching schema.

Schema fields per reframe:
- bottleneck: string
- assumption: string
- reframe: string
- question: string
- measure: string
- compute_after: string
- exact: string
- expected: string
- fails_if: string
- closest_prior: string

Let me think about the domain.

Green–Kubo MD: viscosity from integrating the stress autocorrelation function (SACF) over an equilibrium MD trajectory; thermal conductivity from heat-flux autocorrelation. Statistical convergence of GK transport coefficients is notoriously slow; viscosity uncertainty decays slowly, needs long trajectories or many replicas. The problem's compute unit: six 5-ns replicas per molecule. The bottleneck for ranking: force-field error floor (~25%), which more replicas/longer runs cannot fix — it's a bias, not variance. So more compute buys only more of the same (tighter error bars around a biased value).

Where does more compute stop helping:
1. Force-field systematic bias: error floor ~25%, chemistry-dependent. More sampling doesn't reduce bias. That's the hypothesis itself.
2. GK statistical noise: viscosity autocorrelation has long-time tail; 5 ns × 6 replicas may be insufficient for heavy C30–C50 molecules (viscosities up to 50 mPa·s). For heavy molecules, the SACF decays slowly; 5 ns may not capture the tail, causing truncation bias. More compute (longer runs) could help there — but that's still "more of the same" sequential sampling; wall-clock is the issue. Actually longer runs = more sequential time. Parallel-in-time could help? Hmm, but the system prompt's framing is about reframing so compute changes the answer — parareal for MD equilibration? MD is chaotic, so parareal fails for the trajectory itself (small errors grow). But for sampling (equilibrium, ergodic, mixing dynamics), the "state" is the distribution, and sampling chains are forgetful — the prompt says "a long sampling chain" is a good candidate. So one reframe: instead of one long sequential trajectory, use ensemble/parallel sampling — but the problem already does 6 replicas. The question is whether the unit of work (5 ns replica) is the right one.

Reframes to consider:

Reframe 1: Change what is measured — instead of GK on equilibrium trajectories (slow convergence, O(√t) noise), measure viscosity via reverse non-equilibrium MD (rNEMD) or transient-time correlation / Einstein relations, which converge faster per simulated nanosecond. Question: at fixed wall-clock, does rNEMD give lower viscosity standard error than GK for C30–C50 esters? Measure: run both on ~10 molecules spanning the viscosity range; compare standard error of viscosity per GPU-hour. Cheapest measurement: a few GPU-hours on 3 molecules (C10, C30, C50): maybe $10–20. Compute after: if rNEMD is e.g. 5–10× more efficient for viscosity, then the 120-molecule scan becomes much cheaper or more precise; compute lever becomes real for ranking heavy molecules.

Reframe 2: Change the unit of work — the error floor hypothesis says chemistry-dependent bias. Instead of one fixed force field (LOPLS-AA) scored against measurement, treat force-field parameters as the unit: fit/correct a small set of transferable parameters (or a per-chemistry-class correction) on the 8-molecule published set and test transfer to 120. But "restructuring: none" and the plan expects "not the lever". Hmm, the task asks for reframings that let more compute change the answer. A reframe: replace absolute transport coefficients with relative differences (Δ between molecule pairs) — systematic bias may cancel in differences, so ranking could be good even if absolute error is 25%. Question: does the force field's viscosity error correlate across chemically similar molecules so that pairwise differences rank correctly? Measure: compute Spearman rank and pairwise ordering accuracy on the published 8 molecules + ~12 more; cheapest: reuse published data [s_ogbomo_md] — near zero compute, just reanalysis; cost ~$0 (analyst time). That's the cheapest measurement: reanalyze existing 8-molecule data for rank correlation and pairwise sign agreement. Compute after: if pairwise ordering accuracy is high, more molecules (120) directly tests ranking at scale — compute buys new information.

Reframe 3: Change the objective — instead of ranking by viscosity/thermal conductivity individually, rank by a composite figure of merit for immersion cooling (heat transfer coefficient, pumping power) and ask whether the FOM ranking is robust to 25% errors; or change objective from "rank all molecules" to "screen: classify top decile vs rest". Compute then goes to enlarging the candidate pool screened (835 molecules) because per-molecule cost drops once bias correction is calibrated. Question: is the top-decile membership stable when each molecule's computed properties are perturbed by the measured error floor? Measure: bootstrap/sensitivity reanalysis of the 8-molecule data + database properties; cheap, ~$0–5 (analytic). Hmm but that doesn't consume compute.

Reframe 3 alternative (order of steps): Do cheap coarse screening first (group-contribution / ML model trained on the 835-molecule reference set with measured data) to select the 120 molecules most informative for testing the error-floor hypothesis (active learning / optimal design), rather than a fixed ladder 8/24/48/120. More compute then buys information per molecule chosen adaptively. Question: does an actively chosen 24-molecule set reduce uncertainty in the bias-correction model as much as a randomly chosen 48-molecule set? Measure: simulate the selection on existing data (8 molecules + reference database with measured properties) — cheap, ~$1–5.

Reframe about wall-clock/parallelism per system prompt: The 5-ns sequential trajectory is the unit; for heavy molecules the SACF tail needs longer. Reframe: replace "longer single trajectories" with "many short decorrelated replicas + Green–Kubo with tail model" — that's already partly done (6 replicas). Or use the parareal idea: equilibrium MD sampling is forgetful (mixing), so time-parallel sampling... Actually the standard answer: for sampling, independent replicas side-by-side already parallelize perfectly, so parareal wins nothing (the prompt says check existing GPU methods; also "if thousands of runs are needed, run them side by side instead"). The problem already runs replicas side by side on GPUs. So the parallel-in-time lever is weak here. The real stop: bias floor and slow GK convergence for viscous heavy molecules.

Let me structure three reframes:

Reframe A (what is measured): switch viscosity estimator from Green–Kubo integration of SACF to reverse NEMD (or Einstein–Helfand), which for viscous liquids converges with far less sampling; keeps everything else. Bottleneck: for C30–C50, 30 ns total sampling leaves large GK variance and truncation bias in the SACF tail, so the measured "error floor" mixes force-field bias with estimator noise; more replicas of 5 ns buy only √N noise reduction on a possibly biased tail. Assumption: the 25% floor is a force-field bias independent of estimator and sampling length. Question: for a C40+ molecule at 40 °C, what fraction of the 25% deviation from measurement remains when viscosity is computed by rNEMD with uncertainty <3%? Measure: 3 molecules (light, mid, heavy) × both estimators; ~10 GPU-hours? Cost: at ~$16/machine-hour ($940.98/59 h ≈ $16/h), 10 h ≈ $160. Hmm, budget. Cheapest measurement: run rNEMD on the heaviest 2 published molecules only, 2–4 GPU-hours, ~$30–60. Let's say ~$50. Compute after: if estimator removes most of the gap on heavy molecules, then longer/more runs become the lever and the 120-molecule scan's ranking conclusion changes; compute scales the scan to 835.

Reframe B (what is measured / objective): score pairwise ordering and rank correlation instead of absolute error; systematic bias may cancel. Bottleneck: the plan's pass/fail is set on held-out absolute error (15% / 25%), but the downstream task is ranking; absolute error could stay at 25% while rank correlation is 0.9. Assumption: absolute error floor caps ranking (the hypothesis conflates them). Question: on the published 8 molecules, what is the pairwise ordering accuracy for viscosity and thermal conductivity, and does it exceed 0.9? Measure: pure reanalysis of published data; ~$0. Compute after: if pairwise ordering is already high, compute buys molecules (more pairs = sharper rank statistics), and the 120-molecule run directly measures ranking; the lever is real.

Reframe C (order of steps / unit of work): adaptive molecule selection — choose molecules to maximize information about the bias model (stratify by chemistry class and viscosity decade) instead of fixed ladder; or screen 835 with a cheap ML predictor and only MD the informative ones. Question: does a 24-molecule stratified/active set estimate the bias-correction slope as well as a random 48-molecule set (measured as held-out correction residual)? Measure: resampling study on the reference database (835 molecules with measured properties): fit correction on subsets; ~$1 of CPU, i.e., essentially free; or if needing MD, pilot 12 molecules ~$60. Compute after: if yes, the same $941 covers more chemistry or the full 835 screening with ML prefilter; compute buys coverage, not repetition.

Also could include a reframe on unit of work: replica length. Six 5-ns replicas vs e.g. 60 × 0.5 ns: for forgetful sampling, short replicas from decorrelated starts give the same GK integral with better parallel scaling (more side-by-side), reducing wall-clock per molecule. Question: does the SACF of a C40 ester decorrelate within 2 ns, so that 0.5-ns segments started from decorrelated frames reproduce the 5-ns GK viscosity within 5%? Measure: one molecule, one long run analyzed by block averages; ~$5–15. This aligns with the system prompt (forgetfulness measured by perturbation/decorrelation). Good — the system prompt explicitly suggests measuring forgetfulness. Maybe merge this into Reframe A or make it its own.

We can give up to three. Choose the three strongest, distinct across the axes (what is measured; objective; unit of work/order):

1. Estimator change (what is measured): rNEMD vs GK — tests whether the "error floor" is partly estimator/truncation for heavy molecules. 
2. Objective change: pairwise ordering / rank-first scoring — reanalysis nearly free.
3. Unit of work: replica length and decorrelation — measure SACF decorrelation time τ; if τ ≪ 5 ns, many short replicas from decorrelated starts = same answer with perfect side-by-side parallelism and lower wall-clock; if τ ~ 5 ns, the 5-ns unit is wrong for heavy molecules and compute (longer runs) is the real lever. Question: what is the SACF decorrelation time for the heaviest molecule at 40 °C, and does the GK viscosity plateau by that time? Cheapest measure: one 20-ns run of the C50 molecule, block analysis; ~2–4 GPU-hours ~$30–60.

Hmm, but 2 and 3 both near-free; fine.

Fields per item:

- bottleneck: where more compute stops helping / buys more of the same.
- assumption: the assumption in the current plan that the reframe challenges.
- reframe: description of change.
- question: specific, answerable by measurement, naming what is measured.
- measure: cheapest measurement + rough cost.
- compute_after: what compute buys if the measurement supports the reframe.
- exact: exact pass criterion / what exactly is computed. Hmm "exact" — probably "the exact result is what the loop would give"? In this schema context, "exact" likely means the precise quantitative criterion or exact protocol. I'll interpret: the exact quantitative check/criterion (numbers). 
- expected: expected outcome.
- fails_if: condition under which the reframe fails / not worth pursuing.
- closest_prior: closest prior work, e.g., [s_ogbomo_md] 8 molecules GK, or known literature: rNEMD (Müller-Plathe), etc. Use citation style from the text where possible: [s_ogbomo_md], [s_ogbomo_res], [s_ogbomo_db], and general knowledge like Müller-Plathe 1997 rNEMD.

Let me draft numbers: budget math: $940.98 over 59 machine-hours ⇒ ~$15.95/machine-hour (GPU-hour presumably). Six 5-ns replicas per molecule. Throughput unknown "measured after $36.20 of spend".

Cost estimates:
- Reframe 2 reanalysis: $0 (analyst time; uses published [s_ogbomo_md] numbers).
- Reframe 3: one 20-ns run on the heaviest published molecule (e.g., C50 or squalane-like), 1 replica: a 5-ns replica costs roughly $940.98/(120×6)≈$1.31 per replica at full scale? Actually total plan covers 8+24+48+120? No — run "on 8, 24, 48 then 120 molecules" — that's cumulative sets, total 200 molecule-sets? The $940.98 covers all four levels × 6 replicas × 5 ns = (8+24+48+120)=200 molecules ×6=1200 replica-runs of 5 ns. So per 5-ns replica ≈ $0.78, and 59 machine-hours /1200 runs ≈ 0.05 h per 5-ns replica — that seems too fast for C50. Whatever; rough: a single 20-ns run ≈ 4 replica-equivalents ≈ $3–6, plus analysis. Say ~$5–20. Cheapest: reuse the Check-first 8-molecule runs — append one 20-ns run: ~$5.

- Reframe 1 rNEMD pilot: 2 heavy molecules (e.g., C40, C50 esters from the published 8), each needing a few independent rNEMD runs for statistics: ~10–20 replica-equivalents ≈ $10–30. Say ~$25.

Compute_after statements:
1. If rNEMD removes heavy-molecule gap: 120-molecule scan recosted with rNEMD; compute buys precision on heavy molecules where GK stalls; possibly extend to full 835 screen since per-molecule cost drops.
2. If pairwise ordering already ≥0.9 at n=8: compute goes to more molecules, each new molecule adds O(n) pair comparisons; the ranking question becomes answerable and compute is the lever for rank confidence at 835 scale.
3. If τ small: replace 6×5 ns with ~60×0.5 ns from decorrelated starts; wall-clock per molecule drops ~10× (perfect side-by-side), so the whole ladder finishes in hours; compute then buys molecules, not trajectory length. If τ large: the 5-ns unit is invalid for heavy molecules and longer runs are mandatory — compute is the lever but sequential wall-clock per molecule grows.

Exact criteria:
1. exact: rNEMD and GK viscosities for the same two molecules each with standard error ≤3%; compare both against measured value; report gap GK−measured vs rNEMD−measured.
2. exact: pairwise ordering accuracy = fraction of the 28 molecule pairs whose measured viscosity order is reproduced; also for thermal conductivity; Spearman ρ.
3. exact: normalized SACF ⟨C(t)⟩/C(0) from 0 to 20 ns in 0.5-ns blocks; τ where it falls below e^{-1} (or below 0.05); GK running integral plateau value vs 5-ns truncation value.

fails_if:
1. fails_if: rNEMD deviation from measurement equals GK deviation within uncertainty → floor is force field, estimator swap buys nothing.
2. fails_if: pairwise ordering <0.8 at n=8 (bias not systematic/shared) → ranking is capped and no reframing of scoring helps; or the 8 molecules are too few to conclude (then need ~24).
3. fails_if: SACF has a long tail beyond 5 ns for heavy molecules with the integral still rising at truncation → short replicas inherit truncation bias; only longer sequential runs help.

closest_prior:
1. Müller-Plathe reverse-NEMD viscosity for alkanes (1997–1999); known ~10× efficiency over GK for viscous fluids. Cite as literature knowledge; also [s_ogbomo_md] used GK only.
2. [s_ogbomo_md] itself — 8-molecule data exist; the reanalysis needs no new runs. 
3. Standard GK convergence studies (e.g., SACF tail analyses for viscous liquids); [s_ogbomo_md] used 6×5 ns; closest prior = the plan's own check-first replicate.

Also mention the system-prompt lens? The instructions say find reframings of what is measured, unit of work, objective, order of steps. I'll cover: what-is-measured (estimator), objective (rank-first), unit-of-work/order (replica length + adaptive selection). Three items max. I could fold adaptive selection into fails or compute_after. Let me pick:

R1: estimator (what is measured) — rNEMD.
R2: objective — pairwise/rank scoring with bias cancelation.
R3: unit of work + order of steps — decorrelation-length-based replica sizing; if short, massively parallel short replicas; includes forgetfulness measurement per the lens.

Write each field concisely but completely.

Also note "compute_after" should say whether and how compute becomes the lever after the reframe.

JSON: single object {"reframes":[ {...}, {...}, {...} ]}. Ensure valid JSON, no trailing commas, escape nothing weird. Use plain ASCII mostly; avoid special characters like · — fine in JSON strings (UTF-8 ok). Keep strings self-contained.

Draft:

R1:
bottleneck: "The plan spends nearly all budget repeating the same Green–Kubo estimator; for the heavy C30–C50 liquids the stress autocorrelation decays slowly, so six 5-ns replicas truncate the tail and the measured 25% 'floor' confounds force-field bias with estimator truncation and sampling noise. More identical replicas only shrink variance as 1/sqrt(N) around a possibly truncated integral."
assumption: "That the 25% deviation from measurement is a pure force-field error, independent of how viscosity is extracted and of run length."
reframe: "Change what is measured: compute viscosity by reverse non-equilibrium MD (Muller-Plathe momentum swap) on the same force field and boxes, which for viscous liquids converges with far less sampling than Green–Kubo, and compare both estimators against measurement on the heaviest published molecules."
question: "For the two most viscous molecules in the published eight, does rNEMD with standard error under 3% move the deviation from measurement by more than 5 percentage points relative to the Green–Kubo value?"
measure: "Run rNEMD on the two heaviest published molecules (3 independent runs each) plus one GK replica for control; about 20 replica-equivalents, roughly $25–30 (under 5% of budget)."
compute_after: "If the estimator changes the deviation, per-molecule cost for heavy molecules drops or bias attribution changes, and the 120-molecule scan is recosted with the better estimator; compute then buys coverage toward the 835-molecule set instead of repeated GK noise."
exact: "Report, per molecule: GK viscosity (6x5 ns), rNEMD viscosity with SE from 3 runs, measured value; pass if |rNEMD - measured| differs from |GK - measured| by >5 points on either heavy molecule."
expected: "GK under-converges for the heaviest molecules (tail truncated at 5 ns), so rNEMD shifts their values by 5–15% and part of the 'floor' is estimator, not force field."
fails_if: "rNEMD and GK agree within 3% and both sit ~25% off measurement — then the floor is the force field and no estimator change helps; spend should shift to force-field correction, not sampling."
closest_prior: "Muller-Plathe 1997 reverse-NEMD validated on alkanes and known to outperform Green–Kubo for viscous fluids; [s_ogbomo_md] used Green–Kubo only."

R2:
bottleneck: "Pass/fail is set on held-out absolute error, but the downstream task is ranking coolants; if the force field's error is shared across chemically similar molecules it cancels in pairwise comparisons, so the plan may declare 'not the lever' while the ranking it feeds is already fine — or vice versa. More molecules under the current objective buy tighter estimates of an absolute error that may not cap ranking."
assumption: "That a ~25% absolute error floor caps rank correlation (the hypothesis treats error floor and ranking as the same cap)."
reframe: "Change the objective: score pairwise ordering accuracy and Spearman rank of computed vs measured properties first, and treat absolute error as a secondary diagnostic; test whether ordering is already good at n=8."
question: "On the published eight molecules, what fraction of the 28 viscosity pairs and 28 thermal-conductivity pairs are ordered correctly, and is Spearman rho >= 0.9 for either property?"
measure: "Pure reanalysis of the published eight-molecule table [s_ogbomo_md]; no new simulation, about $0 (analyst hours only)."
compute_after: "If pairwise ordering is already >=0.9, every additional molecule adds O(n) pair tests, so compute directly sharpens rank confidence and the 120-molecule run becomes the decisive ranking measurement; if ordering is poor, ranking is truly capped and compute should go to force-field improvement instead of more molecules."
exact: "Compute pairwise ordering accuracy and Spearman/Kendall rank correlation of MD vs measured viscosity and thermal conductivity for the eight molecules, with bootstrap confidence intervals over resampled molecules."
expected: "Viscosity ordering is strong (rho ~0.9) despite ~25% absolute error because the error is monotonic in chain length; thermal conductivity ordering is weaker."
fails_if: "Pairwise ordering accuracy below ~0.8 at n=8, or bootstrap intervals too wide to decide — then ranking is capped by chemistry-dependent scatter and more molecules under this force field only confirm the cap."
closest_prior: "[s_ogbomo_md] eight-molecule comparison itself; the reordering analysis needs no data beyond it."

R3:
bottleneck: "The unit of work is fixed at 5-ns sequential replicas; wall-clock per molecule is set by the longest chain, and nobody has measured whether 5 ns is too long (sampling wasted) or too short (tail truncated) for the heavy molecules. More compute spent in 5-ns units buys only more of the same unit."
assumption: "That 5 ns is the right replica length for all C10–C50 molecules and that replicas must be long because decorrelation is slow."
reframe: "Change the unit of work and the order of steps: first measure the forgetfulness of the sampling chain — the stress-autocorrelation decay time and the GK running-integral plateau for the heaviest molecule — then size replicas to a few decorrelation times; if that is much shorter than 5 ns, replace 6 long replicas with many short decorrelated-started replicas run side by side, cutting wall-clock per molecule."
question: "For the heaviest published molecule at 40 C, at what time does the normalized stress autocorrelation fall below 0.05, and does the Green–Kubo running viscosity integral reach a plateau (change < 5% over the last half) before 5 ns?"
measure: "Append one 20-ns run of the heaviest molecule to the check-first replicate (about 4 replica-equivalents, roughly $5–10) and block-analyze the autocorrelation and running integral; no new setup needed."
compute_after: "If the plateau is reached well before 5 ns, replicas shrink and multiply: the same budget buys 5–10x more molecules or replicas with perfect side-by-side parallelism, so compute becomes the lever for coverage of the 835-molecule set. If the integral is still rising at 5 ns, the current unit underestimates heavy-molecule viscosity, longer runs are mandatory, and the ladder must drop molecule count to afford them."
exact: "From the 20-ns trajectory report: SACF normalized to its t=0 value vs time; time to fall below 0.05; GK running integral at 1, 2, 5, 10, 20 ns; fractional change between 5 ns and the plateau."
expected: "For C50-sized molecules the SACF tail runs to several ns and the 5-ns integral misses 10–20% of the viscosity; for C10 it plateaus under 1 ns, so one replica length fits all is wrong at both ends."
fails_if: "The running integral is still rising at 20 ns for the heaviest molecules — then viscosity at 40 C needs runs too long to parallelize away, and the honest fix is an estimator change (R1) or accepting a heavy-molecule bias."
closest_prior: "Standard Green–Kubo convergence studies showing slow SACF tails for long-chain alkanes; the plan's own check-first replicate of [s_ogbomo_md] provides the launch point."

That's three solid reframes across measured-quantity, objective, unit-of-work/order. Costs roughly consistent with plan economics ($940.98/59h ≈ $16/machine-hour; per 5-ns replica ≈ $0.8 if 1200 replicas... my "replica-equivalents" cost claims: 20 replica-equivalents ≈ $16 if $0.8 each; I said $25–30 — fine as rough. 4 replica-equivalents ≈ $3–5; I said $5–10 — fine.)

Also the system prompt says: check whether a strong GPU method already exists. I can nod to that in fails_if or compute_after of R3 (side-by-side replicas already parallel; the win is sizing, not a new parallel scheme). Good—mention in R3 compute_after or bottleneck: "replicas already run side by side, so no time-parallel scheme wins; the win is unit sizing."
